# Arthritis

In this worked example, we will be working with data from a double-blind clinical
trial comparing a new treatment for rheumatoid arthritis with a placebo. The
outcome records whether patients showed no, some, or marked improvement. The
[dataset documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/vcd/html/Arthritis.html)
does not name the specific treatment.

The data comes from the [vcd package](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=vcd).
To begin, let's load the package and take a `glimpse()` at the data.

```{r}
# install.packages("vcd") # if you haven't installed it yet
library(vcd)
library(tidyverse)

glimpse(Arthritis)
```

Notice that `Improved` is helpfully formatted as an ordinal (ordered) variable
already, which is going to help ggplot to choose the correct color palettes for
us.

# Bar Charts

Let's start with a simple bar chart to see how many people were allocated to the
two treatment arms.

```{r, fig.width = 2.2, fig.height = 2.2}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(Arthritis, aes(Treatment)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Was the Treatment Effective?

Now for something more interesting. Let's try to look at how well the treatment
seems to have worked. We start with a stacked bar chart.

```{r, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(Arthritis, aes(x = Treatment, fill = Improved)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black") +
  labs(fill = "Improvement") # add a better legend title
```

It's immediately clear that the treatment has worked well! The count of people
with an improvement is much higher in the treatment arm compared with the placebo
arm. But how do the treatments compare in terms of people who've made
*some* improvement? This is difficult to say from our approach here. This
is due to two reasons:

1. The stacked bar chart makes it hard to compare all but the
   bottom segment (`Marked` here), since the other portions of the bars are not aligned.^[This
   is not quite as severe a problem for this particular visualization since the
   inner grouping variable is ordinal. For other problems, however, this can
   be much more detrimental to the result.]
2. The bars are not proportional.^[To be fair, the differences between the group
   sizes are small here, but this also means that we don't lose much information
   when using proportional bars instead.]

Let's try a grouped proportional bar chart instead. To achieve this, we need
to do a little preparatory work, since ggplot2 does not offer a direct option for this purpose.

What we need to do is to prepare a data set with the proportions that we would
like to plot. In the following lines, we

1. use `count()` to count the number of observations in each combination of
   `Treatment` and `Improved`,
2. group the data set by `Treatment`, and
3. compute the proportions using `mutate()`.

```{r}
arthritis_prop <-
  Arthritis %>%
  count(Treatment, Improved) %>% # like group_by + summarize
  group_by(Treatment) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

Now, we're ready to construct our plot. This will be done similarly to a standard
grouped bar plot, except we will use `geom_col()` and map the `y` aesthetic, as we
are working with summary data.

```{r, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(arthritis_prop, aes(Treatment, prop, fill = Improved)) +
  geom_col(color = "black", position = "dodge") +
  labs(fill = "Improvement", y = "Proportion")
```

Now, it becomes quite easy to compare the proportion of people who showed some improvement between the two groups. 

See if you can also create a proportional stacked bar chart and compare the
result with your previous charts.

## A Larger Example with Unequal Groups

Both problems are more visible in `DanishWelfare`, also supplied by **vcd**.
We will compare place of residence (`Urban`) across marital-status groups
(`Status`). The [dataset](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/vcd/html/DanishWelfare.html)
already contains frequencies in `Freq`, so we sum those counts. We also give
the categories more readable labels using `fct_recode()` from **forcats**,
which is loaded with **tidyverse**. This function renames factor levels using
`new_label = "old_label"`. For example, `Widowed = "Widow"` changes the label
`"Widow"` to `"Widowed"`. The category counts and factor order are preserved.

```{r welfare-summary}
welfare_summarized <-
  DanishWelfare %>%
  group_by(Status, Urban) %>%
  summarize(Count = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    Status = fct_recode(Status, Widowed = "Widow"),
    Urban = fct_recode(Urban,
                       "Copenhagen suburbs" = "SubCopenhagen",
                       "Large cities" = "LargeCity",
                       "Other cities" = "City",
                       "Countryside" = "Country")
  )

welfare_prop <-
  welfare_summarized %>%
  group_by(Status) %>%
  mutate(prop = Count / sum(Count))

# Keep the same residence colors in the bar charts, mosaic, and waffles.
welfare_colors <- c("Copenhagen" = "darkorange",
                    "Copenhagen suburbs" = "skyblue",
                    "Large cities" = "goldenrod",
                    "Other cities" = "seagreen",
                    "Countryside" = "orchid")
```

```{r welfare-bars, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%", fig.width = 4.8, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(welfare_prop, aes(Status, Count, fill = Urban)) +
  geom_col(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Stacked counts", x = "Marital status",
       y = "Count", fill = "Residence")

ggplot(welfare_prop, aes(Status, prop, fill = Urban)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Grouped proportions", x = "Marital status",
       y = "Proportion within group", fill = "Residence")
```

The groups contain 580 widowed, 3,633 married, and 931 unmarried respondents.
With five colored segments and such different totals, the floating segments
are harder to compare. For example, the married group has **more Copenhagen
residents** than the widowed group (288 versus 116), but Copenhagen represents
a **smaller proportion** of that group (7.9% versus 20%). The grouped
proportional chart makes both the denominator and the common baseline clear.

# Mosaic Plots

In the lecture, we also encountered mosaic plots. These extend proportional
stacked bar charts by allowing the widths of the bars to vary with the relative
group sizes. We'll use the **ggmosaic2** package here.

```{r}
# install.packages("ggmosaic2") # if you don't already have the package

library(ggmosaic2)
```

**ggmosaic2** works directly with a ggplot2 object,
adding auxiliary functions (`geom_*()` functions) to extend its functionality.

```{r}
ggplot(Arthritis) +
  geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(Improved, Treatment), fill = Improved))
```

The key features to notice about this call are

1. that we supply the `aes()` mapping to `geom_mosaic()` in this example,
   with `fill = Improved` determining the colors, and
2. the call to `product(Improved, Treatment)`, which lists the variables from
   the inner subdivision to the outer grouping. With the default layout,
   `Treatment` determines the widths of the bars, and `Improved` subdivides each
   bar vertically.

Read the dimensions of this plot as follows:

- The **width** of each treatment bar represents that arm's share of all
  participants.
- The **height** of each colored segment represents the proportion of
  participants in that improvement category *within that treatment arm*.
- The **area** of each rectangle is proportional to the share of all
  participants with that combination of treatment and improvement.

For example, 21 of the 41 treated participants showed `Marked` improvement.
The height of their segment therefore represents `21 / 41`, while its area
represents `21 / 84`, since there are 84 participants in total.

The mosaic plot therefore shows both the relative sizes of the treatment arms
and their improvement proportions in a single plot.^[These are relative sizes.
To communicate the actual sample sizes, also provide the counts in the text.]

Try switching the order to `product(Treatment, Improved)`. Which variable now
determines the widths? What proportions do the vertical subdivisions show?
Which ordering makes it easier to compare improvement between treatment arms?

## A Mosaic Plot for the Danish Welfare Data

The unequal group sizes in `DanishWelfare` are more visible in a mosaic plot.
We reuse `welfare_summarized` and its residence colors. Since each row contains
an aggregated count, `weight = Count` makes the rectangles represent
respondents rather than rows in the summary table.

```{r welfare-mosaic, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(welfare_summarized) +
  geom_mosaic(aes(x = product(Urban, Status), fill = Urban, weight = Count)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Marital status", y = "Residence", fill = "Residence")
```

The widths represent the marital-status group sizes, while the segment heights
represent residence proportions within each group. For example, the married
group is much wider, but its Copenhagen segment is shorter than that of the
widowed group (7.9% versus 20%). Its Copenhagen rectangle still has a larger
area because it represents more respondents (288 versus 116). The mosaic
therefore displays both group size and composition, although the interior
segments still lack a common baseline for comparing their heights.

# Waffle Plots

Waffle plots are easy-to-read visualizations that, while quite uncommon
in statistical visualizations, are much more prevalent in media outlets such as
newspapers. As we mentioned in the lecture, they are at their best when some of
the categories are so small that their sizes are hard to estimate in a
bar chart or mosaic plot.

For this example, install **waffle** from
[GitHub](https://github.com/hrbrmstr/waffle) using the **remotes** package.
Run these installation commands once before continuing.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#install.packages("remotes") # if you haven't already installed it
library(remotes)
#remotes::install_github("hrbrmstr/waffle")
```

For a count waffle, we first need the number of participants in each category.
Group the data by `Improved` and `Treatment`, then use `summarize()` together
with `n()` to compute the counts. Before
looking at the following code, see if you can do this by yourself. The result
should be a 6-row tibble with columns `Treatment`, `Improved` and `Count` (or
whatever you want to call it). Save the result to an object called
`arthritis_summarized`.

```{r}
arthritis_summarized <-
  Arthritis %>%
  group_by(Treatment, Improved) %>%
  summarize(Count = n())
head(arthritis_summarized)
```

Now we're ready to start making waffles! The aesthetics you need to know about
here are `fill` and `values`. Mapping `Count` to `values` means that **one square
represents one participant**, while `fill = Improved` determines the colors.
We start with the simplest possible waffle chart, just looking at improvement
among the participants in the treatment arm.

```{r}
library(waffle)

filter(arthritis_summarized, Treatment == "Treated") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = Improved, values = Count)) +
  geom_waffle() +
  labs(fill = "Improvement")
```

The treated group contains 13 participants with `None`, 7 with `Some`, and 21
with `Marked` improvement. The plot therefore has 41 squares. Each square
represents `100 / 41` percent, or about 2.44% of the treated group.

This looks kind of like a waffle chart, but there's a lot of superfluous
information that we'd rather get rid of. Thankfully, **waffle** provides the
helpful `theme_enhance_waffle()` function for this. Moreover, we probably prefer
the symbols (rectangles) to be squares --- it's supposed to look like a waffle
after all, right? --- which we can accomplish by forcing the coordinate system to
be isometric using `coord_equal()`. Finally, I think it looks more aesthetically
pleasing if we swap the black line color for white, increase their widths
slightly, and change theme to the minimal variant.

```{r}
filter(arthritis_summarized, Treatment == "Treated") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fill = Improved, values = Count)) +
  geom_waffle(color = "white", size = 1.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme_enhance_waffle() +
  labs(fill = "Improvement",
       subtitle = "Treated group: one square = one participant")
```

This looks much better, doesn't it?

To be able to use waffle charts to see both of the treatment arms at once,
we need to use something called **facets**, which we haven't covered in the
course yet. If you already know about facets, however, feel free to 
modify the plot now by faceting on the type of treatment.

## Counts and Percentages with More Data

Let's return to `DanishWelfare` and select the **3,633 married respondents**.
A count waffle needs one square for each respondent. A percentage waffle uses
100 squares for the whole group, so one square represents 1%.

```{r welfare-percentages}
welfare_married <-
  welfare_summarized %>%
  filter(Status == "Married") %>%
  mutate(Percent = 100 * Count / sum(Count),
         Squares = round(Percent))

welfare_married
#sum(welfare_married$Squares)
```

Here, rounding gives 8, 12, 12, 34, and 34 percentage squares, which sum to 100.
Check this sum when using other data: ordinary rounding does not always give
exactly 100 squares. We use 60 squares per full row for the count waffle and
a 10-by-10 grid for the percentage waffle. `flip = TRUE` fills the rows
horizontally.

```{r welfare-waffle-comparison, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 160}
welfare_count_plot <-
  ggplot(welfare_married, aes(fill = Urban, values = Count)) +
  geom_waffle(n_rows = 60, flip = TRUE, color = "white", size = 0.15) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme_enhance_waffle() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Counts: 3,633 squares", fill = "Residence",
       subtitle = "One square = one respondent")

welfare_percent_plot <-
  ggplot(welfare_married, aes(fill = Urban, values = Squares)) +
  geom_waffle(n_rows = 10, flip = TRUE, color = "white", size = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme_enhance_waffle() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Percentages: 100 squares", fill = "Residence",
       subtitle = "One square = 1% of the married group")

welfare_count_plot
welfare_percent_plot
```

The count waffle preserves every respondent, but the many small squares make
it dense. The percentage waffle makes the composition easier to read, at the
cost of rounding. For example, 430 respondents from Copenhagen suburbs and
419 from large cities both become 12 percentage squares.

## Comparing Three Groups

Now show count waffles for all three marital-status groups.
`facet_wrap(~ Status)` gives each group its own panel. With fixed scales and
the same number of squares per full row, squares have the same size in every
panel.

```{r welfare-waffle-groups, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, dpi = 160}
welfare_groups_plot <-
  ggplot(welfare_summarized, aes(fill = Urban, values = Count)) +
  geom_waffle(n_rows = 50, flip = TRUE, color = "white", size = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ Status, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = welfare_colors) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme_enhance_waffle() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(fill = "Residence", subtitle = "One square = one respondent")

welfare_groups_plot
```

The interpretation issues remain. The married group has a larger waffle
because it has more respondents, and its 288 Copenhagen squares still
correspond to a smaller share than the 116 Copenhagen squares in the widowed
group. The other colored regions begin at different positions, making their
sizes harder to compare. Percentage waffles would adjust for group size,
but grouped proportional bars also give every category a common baseline.
